cues.text: Section eight.
The IT service desk and ITSM.
A service desk is the central contact point between users and IT support.
It logs issues, classifies requests, prioritises work, communicates status, resolves or escalates incidents, and records knowledge.
You may also hear the term help desk.
A help desk often focuses on technical troubleshooting, whereas a service desk has a broader service-management role.
Now let us look at the incident workflow.
It runs in this order: detect and log, then categorise, then prioritise, then diagnose, then resolve or escalate, then restore service, and finally confirm and close.
Escalation comes in two forms.
Functional escalation sends work to specialists.
Hierarchical escalation involves management when authority or urgency requires it.
Next, priority.
Priority is commonly determined by impact and urgency.
A widespread outage with immediate business consequences receives higher priority than an individual cosmetic issue.
Keep in mind that severity and priority may differ under local policy.
Now to the agreements that govern service.
A service level agreement, or SLA, defines agreed service expectations, such as availability, response and resolution targets.
An operational level agreement, or OLA, coordinates the internal teams that support the SLA.
An underpinning contract defines commitments with external suppliers.
Here is an example showing how these fit together.
The customer-facing SLA promises restoration within four hours.
An internal OLA requires the database team to respond within 30 minutes, and a vendor contract requires infrastructure support within one hour.
These commitments must fit together, so that the internal and supplier promises make the customer-facing promise achievable.
Now, metrics.
Common metrics include first contact resolution, or FCR, mean time to restore service, ticket backlog, SLA attainment, and customer satisfaction.
For SLA attainment, if 90 of 100 eligible tickets meet SLA targets, attainment is 90 percent.
One caution: a high closure count is not evidence of quality if users repeatedly reopen tickets.
Finally, the configuration management database, or CMDB.
A CMDB records configuration items and the relationships between them.
Knowing which applications depend on a database helps you assess incident impact and plan changes.
